speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the policy of the Department of Communications is to permit common carriers to own and operate satellite earth stations only in the 12/14 Ghz band. This policy may make sense in southern Canada but makes no sense in the Far North where, for technical reasons, it is necessary to use the 4/6 Ghz band. Hence Northwest Tel, the federal Crown corporation providing telecommunications in the North, is obliged to pay exorbitant rents, far in excess of the true value, to Telsat Canada for the use of its facilities. These excessive costs are then passed on to Northwest Tel's subscribers. Therefore, in order to avoid this discrimination against Northern telephone subscribers, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen):
That Northwest Tel Incorporated be permitted to own and operate satellite earth stations in the 4/6 Ghz band.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Hon. Minister of the Environment. Yesterday the Hon. Minister said in the House that he had received telegrams from the Lake Louise-Banff Chamber of Commerce supporting the project. Note that he said "telegrams".
I hold in my hand a copy of the telex that was sent to the Hon. Minister on October 5. The gist of it reads, "We urge your Department to expedite the approval process for this project." The Minister was well aware yesterday that this telex was sent by two men only, one of whom is John Morrison, who is a friend of Judd Buchanan. The other man is President of the Chamber of Commerce and also the solicitor for Judd Buchanan's company. No one else in the Chamber of Commerce knew that this telex was sent until approximately a month later. As soon as the members of the Lake Louise Chamber of Commerce found out about the said telex, another

November 24, 1982

-in answer to that question posed by the Hon. Member. First, I want to make it clear that both the telegram and the representations to which we referred yesterday came to us in October, as he indicated, when the decision on the land transfer had taken place a month earlier. That is to say, these representations, whatever their validity, were a month after the decision for the project had taken place. A decision had been made and, to that degree, they were too late.
The second comment I would like to make is that I know that the hon. gentleman would not want deliberately to mislead the House. He has referred to the telegram as containing the signatures of the people whom he has mentioned. Therefore, I think I should read the telegram, which is quite short, in its entirety. It says:
Attn Hon. John Roberts, Minister of the Environment Re: Block 63, Banff, Alberta T01 0C0
We understand that there have been negotiations regarding a rental accommodation development for Banff. Due to the extreme shortage of employee housing, we urge your Department to expedite the approval process for this project.

Banff-Lake Louise Chamber of Commerce
That is the telegram in its entirety.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Hon. Minister has been told a number of times who sent that telegram. He knows very well. He is the one who is misleading the House. speechtext: Again, Madam Speaker, the hon. gentleman asserts that the telegram was sent by two men. The text clearly indicates that, so far as the recipient knew, it was sent by the Banff-Lake Louise Chamber of Commerce. There are no two names attached to this telegram. That is the name.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES
APPLICATION OF CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister, who will know that his former colleague in Cabinet, the Hon. Judd Buchanan, and his partners, have been actively pursuing this project involving the transfer of Government lands over the course of well over two years. The Prime Minister will also know that the postemployment conflict of interest guidelines demand that former Ministers not be involved with a commercial corporation in connection with any specific proceeding or transaction in which the Government of Canada is a party for two years following their exit from the Ministry. Mr. Buchanan was Minister of Public Works until mid-1979.
Is the Prime Minister going to look into enforcing the conflict of interest guidelines, at least in this instance, with respect to the activities of Mr. Buchanan, a former Minister of his Cabinet?

It seems to me, insofar as I remember the conflict of interest guidelines-I believe they were accurately read by the Hon. Member-they apply to a Minister who leaves a Department and then who would use his knowledge or acquaintance with that Department, or familiarity with people in that Department, to enter into some commercial transaction. If my recollection is right, Mr. Buchanan left the Department responsible for Parks Canada somewhere around 1975 or 1976, so he was well within the guidelines if his initiative was taken about two years ago.

subsubtopic: JOB OPPORTUNITIES FOR OLDER WOMEN
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. An NDP Task Force on Older Women has been holding hearings in every Province. It has been told repeatedly that women who spend their whole lives raising Canada's children, experience extreme poverty, isolation, and loneliness in their middle and later years. On behalf of these women I would like to ask the Minister what plans he has or what he will do to develop job opportunities for mature women. In particular, will he allocate some of the funds available for job-creation programs to target the needs of this age group, these women who really need an opportunity to work and pay into a pension plan?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: JOB OPPORTUNITIES FOR OLDER WOMEN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think the Hon. Member raises a very legitimate and very important concern. I should like to point out to her that in the past year we have taken a number of initiatives to respond directly to that particular problem. In something like 12 centres across Canada we have opened special women's employment centres to provide counselling and placement services as well as special help in the transfer from home to the first-time job.
In addition, we have substantially increased the Outreach budget so that community based organizations can also provide that kind of employment base service to them. As well, the Canada Community Service Employment Program is particularly targetted to this group. Almost 80 per cent of the people working in the Program have worked in child care, in social services programs, or are women coming into the work force for the first time and they are closer to their clientele.

subsubtopic: JOB OPPORTUNITIES FOR OLDER WOMEN
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is important to have counselling support services but there is no point having them if there are no jobs at the end.

I have a supplementary question, Madam Speaker. In connection with the services of the Canada Employment Centres we often find that homemakers are handicapped because they do not have job
experience and so do not have a job reference. It has been proposed by some women that we have heard from, that there could be a testing program carried out at Canada Employment Centres. As a result of this a certificate could be awarded which would recognize the skills of women in human relations and management, and the other skills that they have acquired in a lifetime of experience could also be recognized. Will the Minister implement this in Employment Centres as a means of giving older women a chance for a good resume and then a good chance at a job?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, obviously if we established that particular program it would be to give us information and ideas about how we could more broadly expand those initiatives. We would be prepared to look at such a program and see how we could apply it on a national level.
I would point out again that I know of one project in my own city, an employment counselling service which is an Outreach Program. In the last two or three months it has had something like a 70 per cent success rate, enabling older women entering the work place to find their first jobs. It is a very specific example of how a good counselling placement service, working individually with women, can provide them with both the opportunity to choose how they can upgrade their skills and also get their first job opportunities. This is what we really want to concentrate on, that is, providing individualized service where it is needed most in terms of making that major transition from home to work.

subsubtopic: UNITED STATES DECISION TO DEPLOY MX MISSILES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Defence. On Monday night President Reagan announced his intention to proceed with the development of the MX missile, using a dense-pack basing plan. Would the Minister tell the House if he was advised or briefed on this decision by Washington or by his own staff prior to this announcement, and could he tell us what Canada's position is concerning the feasibility of the proposed dense-pack plan?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: UNITED STATES DECISION TO DEPLOY MX MISSILES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think the communication between Washington and this Government is normally very fluent. 1 think the Department of External Affairs was aware of the deliberations of the President concerning the MX missiles and also about some of the issues he would address in his speech. I think it is only normal that we in the Department of National Defence, through our contacts with the Department of External Affairs know what is going on between our American friends and ourselves. As far as the issue of the MX missile is conerned, I think it is part of the two-track decision which was taken by NATO to try to create a credible deterrent in order to avoid war and preserve the peace. Actually, that is the basis of all actions taken by the United States within the NATO area.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. Will the Minister now confirm that CTC's legal branch has ruled that this practice is, in fact, completely illegal, and will he now order all charter carriers involved to refund fully, with interest, the moneys illegally withheld? Will he further order them, particularly during the holiday season, to obey the law immediately and stop fleecing thousands of Canadian travellers?

It appears that tour

operators are charging more than 10 per cent and stating that that amount is not refundable, either. That is clearly being done. People can read the conditions. speechtext:

According to press reports, a Government study on gasoline costs has shown that Canadian consumers are being gouged by something like 12 cents a gallon too much for unleaded gas, a fact that I pointed out to the Minister some six months ago. The Minister said in a letter that the high cost of unleaded gas was probably due to the fact that only the prices for regular gasoline were posted at the pumps and, therefore, there really was not any competition.

Now that the Minister has had a year and a half to study the matter, what does he intend to do to bring this environmentally preferable kind of fuel back down to earth?

Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate
Affairs): Madam Speaker, I think that the answer to one of the questions put by the Hon. subsubtopic: FOREIGN AID TO THE U.S.S.R.
speechtext: Since May, 1971, did the Government extend financial aid in any form to the Government of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics for the purpose of partially financing construction of oil and gas pipelines, or for drilling and exploratory well development, or for any other purpose relating to energy extraction, development and supply and, if so, what was the precise nature and level of the financing?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FOREIGN AID TO THE U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
The Canadian Government has not extended any foreign aid to the Government of the U.S.S.R. since 1971. Foreign aid is offered only by the Canadian International Development Agency (CIDA) to developing countries and the U.S.S.R. is not such a country. This having been said, however, official credits in support of Canadian exporters have been provided to the U.S.S.R. by the Export Development Corporation (EDC). in this respect since 1971, the Export Development Corporation provided financing for a total of $253,849,570 to support sixteen different sales of Canadian goods and services to the U.S.S.R. Thirteen of these transactions amounting to $215,224,991 were related to the energy sector. Twelve of them were financed under the Financial Protocol Agreement between EDC and the Ministry of Foreign Trade of the U.S.S.R. dated May 5, 1975 and one was financed under a separate loan agreement in 1974, prior to the signing of the Protocol. In respect of each contract, EDC financing covered 85 per cent of the sale price of the Canadian goods and services. speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Dionne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO REDUCE INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in my view, Bill C-134, an Act respecting rebates of interest on farm loans made under the Farm Credit Act, is essential to the implementation of special measures reintroduced by the Government in its budget last June. As the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) mentioned earlier, the federal Farm Financial Assistance Program was established in order to alleviate the distressing situation created by high interest rates and lower returns on farm products. Canadian farmers who are facing serious financial difficulties can obtain an interest rebate of four percentage points on their loans for two years, which reduces the effective interest cost to 11% per cent during the first two years of the loan. The program has already saved several hundred farmers from bankruptcy, and will probably save several hundred more before it expires.
The Farm Credit Corporation has always done its utmost to help its clients through difficult periods. Its recovery plans, for instance, are among the most flexible known. FCC credit advisers encourage farmers to discuss their financial difficulties as soon as they become apparent, so that they can then reconsider repayment schedules and take appropriate action. In some cases, rescheduling of the loan may be necessary. In others, postponement of one or two payments may be sufficient. It is reassuring to note, however, that the FCC is sufficiently concerned about the problems facing its clients to take this kind of action, and that this agency, which represents the government, has not forgotten the human factor in its business relations with Canadian farmers.
In addition to its flexible recovery plans and the special loans being granted since June 1982 under the Special Farm Financial Assistance Program, the FCC offers its borrowers every opportunity to resolve their financial problems through its Advisory Services Program.
Generally speaking, all FCC loan applicants may benefit from preliminary counselling, including advice on how to organize and develop their farm operations. The service is available to any FCC borrower who asks for it. However, the service is compulsory in the case of borrowers under the special program, since it is one of the conditions of the loan. If we look at the components of this program, it is easy to understand why the service is compulsory for borrowers who are in financial difficulty and are anxious to improve their situation. First of all, the goal of the Advisory Services Program is to help the farmer manage his farm finances more effectively. The credit adviser will therefore help the farmer to select the accounting system that is best adapted to his needs and help him get acquainted with the system.
With his financial training and experience, the credit adviser is also in a position to help the farmer interpret and analyze the financial data provided by his accounting system. He can also provide a comparative analysis of financial factors and farm production in similar operations. Finally, if the farmer requires additional counselling, the credit adviser can tell him where to obtain the information or the help he needs. Thus,
this service is an adjunct to provincial educational programs. As a result of the follow-up provided through the Advisory Services Program, the farmer has a better chance of successfully implementing his recovery plan.
Mr. Speaker-
-a Bill of this nature is not new. In the November 12, 1981 budget speech the then minister of finance announced a similar special program to assist farmers in financial distress. It provided a 5 percentage point rebate. Similar legislation to this Bill came into force in April, 1982 for the November 12, 1981 special program, which terminated on March 31, 1981. There was strong demand for the program, as the statistics indicate. From November 12, 1981 to March 31, 1982, 382 loans totalling $45,417 million were approved. Interest rebates on these loans over a two-year period will total about $4.6 million.
I urge Hon. Members to support this Bill which will be instrumental in assisting so many Canadian farmers through these difficult times. Most agricultural producers are at the mercy of the marketplace for their incomes. The price received for their production does not correspond with their costs, and in recent times costs have outstripped earnings for a significant number of them. I firmly believe that most of these producers can survive and contribute to the economy if they are given a chance to recover. This interest subsidy for a two-year period provides that breathing room. Agriculture is essential for a healthy economy. If our economy is to strengthen, so must agriculture.
[ Translation]
Thus, Mr. Speaker, the FCC is doing everything in its power to help borrowers through the difficult times we are experiencing today. By supporting Bill C-134, my hon. colleagues will enable us to continue its good work.
Mr. Speaker, I trust the debate will be short and that on both sides of the House, Hon. Members will act quickly so that our farmers will be able to take advantage of the benefits of Bill C-134 as soon as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments before we conclude the debate on Bill C-134, a piece of legislation that is indeed important to farmers who, like so many other sectors, are facing tremendous problems because of a bankrupt economy. We are being asked to expedite this bill. Well, I shall be fairly brief, but nevertheless, I would like to remind the Government that the fact we are obliged to consider this kind of legislation, namely Bill C-34, today, means that things are not as they should be in this country, and perhaps the Government should recognize this. As usual, it seems the Government is once again introducing corrective measures at the last minute to save people who are in dire straits because of a lack of economic foresight and
November 24, 1982

probably also because of a lack of adequate economic provisions. Not long ago, we had an interesting debate on the importance of research and development, and considering the significance of agriculture to our economy, I believe that more substantial allocation of funds to more thorough research would have enabled the agricultural sector, which I consider extremely important, to benefit as well from certain legal provisions that in all cases would have helped to alleviate the problems with which farmers are now faced.
In my riding, as is the case in Quebec generally, agriculture ranks fairly high, and it is particularly important because this sector is responsible for 25 per cent of our economy. Therefore,
I need not dwell further on the importance of the agricultural sector. On many occasions, Mr. Speaker, I have heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) talk about the excellent position our farmers are in today. We all know that farm operations have increased tremendously in value. We also know there has also been a tremendous decrease in the number of farmers, while farm production has increased enormously, thanks to modern technology and research. Many people often get the impression that our farmers are now out of the woods. However, we have found that farmers, too, have been affected by the present economic situation.
In Quebec, which in 1951 had 134,000 farms, there are now 48,144 farms. There has therefore been a significant drop in the number of farmers. I agree that we have all these new measures and all these modern techniques and that the Farm Credit Corporation has made it easier for farmers to take advantage of these by facilitating loans, but I still think that farmers are facing a serious problem today. Especially during the last two years, there was a rise in interest rates which hurt them quite badly, and increased production costs. Here are some statistics to illustrate the significance of agriculture. For instance, farm debt increased from $1.6 billion in 1960 to $16 billion in 1981. In 1982, net farm incomes have dropped by 17 per cent. I think that these are some of the basic reasons why production costs have increased.
More specifically, it is known that energy costs represent 25 per cent of a farm's operating costs, and today, that is a lot of money. It is certainly a substantial increase, when we realize that the purchase of oil products alone represents 25 per cent of operating costs in the agricultural sector. In greenhouse operations, for instance, energy costs represent 22 per cent of operating costs, while this is only 14 per cent in dairy operations. I am therefore quite aware that things have changed in the farming sector. We must also recognize that if we have
300,000	farmers in Canada, that represents 500,000 jobs, since we have 4,000 businesses producing food and beverages, which provides employment for another 200,000 Canadians. The agro-food sector represents 40 per cent of our economy and employs 25 per cent of the labour force. Finally, it is also a well-known fact that in 1980, exports of farm products were
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
worth $8 billion compared to $5 billion for imports, meaning an excess trade balance of $3.5 billion.
Mr. Speaker, I think that although this bill will enable farmers to take advantage of a rebate of 4 percentage points, reducing the regular rate of 15% per cent to 11% per cent, the fact remains that it is not enough to ensure continuity and encourage young people to take up farming. I agree that the government is offering very substantial assistance today. I am sorry that no further provision was made other than this last minute measure to cope with an urgent problem, and this comment could apply to many other sectors as well. The fact remains that if we are discussing the survival and expansion of agriculture, we must first take a close look at capital gains policies. This year, we made proposals in this respect, which, if implemented, would have helped farmers. There is no doubt about that. Today, there is increasing talk of a tax credit for energy costs in the agricultural sector, which could help reduce this aspect of production costs. I think we should take a serious look at suggestions made by colleagues here in the House, and I would like to take a few minutes to talk more specifically about our young people, Mr. Speaker.
Times have changed, and increasingly, the family farm is being taken over by strangers or foreigners. The fact remains that the tradition of the family farm has undergone some very profound changes as a result of the increase in value of farming operations. As we all know, some 30, 40 or 50 years ago, it was not unusual for a father to leave the farm to his son, provided he kept it until he died. Today, however, things have changed, and if we consider the value of a farm operation and our present interest rates, how can a young man under 30 purchase a family farm that is worth $300,000, $500,000 and even $1 million in some cases? If special measures are not taken very soon to help young people who want to go into farming, there is very real danger that the number of farmers will continue to drop as it has during the past 10 or 20 years. I am saying this in all objectivity. I have the clear impression, Mr. Speaker, that we need some very specific policies to provide special assistance to young farmers who want to own their own farm operation and make this sector of our economy a prosperous one.
In the circumstances, I wonder whether we will not have to give serious consideration to a special interest rate, and I do mean special, at the risk of appearing to discriminate against other groups, and I wonder, in fact, how we can ensure that these young people will have a future if we do not introduce special measures such as a rate of interest that would appear to discriminate, and I repeat this, against other groups, a privileged interest rate for Canadians under 30 or perhaps 35, but in any case, this is what I would like to suggest today, and I would invite the Government to give careful consideration to a policy that would encourage young people to start their own operation and not only enable them to purchase, but also to keep, their own farm. The Government is going to answer: We

have increased the FCC budget for a number of years, and every time we try to allocate more funds for loans.
Mr. Speaker, I recall having informed the minister in the House on several occasions: You are doing a tremendous job on facilitating loans, but the future of our agriculture does not depend on the availability of loans but on the farmer's profits, and all my hon. colleagues agree with me on this point. Of course, loans are necessary for investment and expansion purposes, and we all understand this. I repeat that if the Government has no policy in the short term for privileged rates for young people some time it will have to set a certain age limit to ensure continuity in this sector. Conditions have changed and times have changed, and young people are no longer able to purchase the family farm and save it for posterity. And that is so important to us in Quebec and to people throughout Canada.
I therefore support the measure presented in the House today. It is at least an attempt to do something. It may be too little, too late, but it had to be done. The house is on fire and we have to call out the fire brigade. The Government is manning the fire engines, but we cannot be choosy when there is a fire. The fact remains that these are stopgap measures, and that we must consider, in the long term, how we can improve agriculture and ensure its survival, how we can give young people a chance, and there are many who are interested, Mr. Speaker. Many representations are made to me in my constituency. In my view, this is a serious concern among the young who need assistance, and within the current context, we have to provide some relief to ensure the survival of farming in Canada.
It is my hope that these brief comments, Mr. Speaker, will be taken very seriously, as I am making them in earnest. We will support this legislation, but feel the government should go further and perhaps fund more advanced research in agriculture so that reliance on emergency measures is no longer necessary. Hopefully this will offer farmers easier access to borrowing, and better opportunities to make a living without requiring the support of the Farm Credit Corporation. It is a good thing they can depend on the Corporation for help but even better if they can do without. I will conclude on this, Mr. Speaker, and let other members make their comments. My feeling is that we will see this legislation through today without further delay.

subtopic: FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO REDUCE INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate briefly in this debate. It is not my intention to hold up passage of the Bill because I support the principle and agree with the premise of the Bill which sets out to reduce the Farm Credit Corporation interest rate up to 4 per cent over a period of two years in circumstances where farmers find themselves in difficulty. I understand that roughly one half of the $200 million has been allocated, and there are roughly 550 farmers who have qualified. That really means that it will be useful to approximately
1,000	farmers and to that extent it is welcome and, of course,
is supported by Members in all corners of the House. But really, it is an example of a half-baked measure being offered to assist a very troubled industry. I think it is designed more to serve the Government as a public relations exercise or as flim-flammery than as an offer of genuine help to the industry. For instance, it does not compare to the magnitude of a Maislin, a Chrysler, a Canadair or a Dome bailout. It relegates agriculture to a second or third rate position, and I take exception to that.
In the last couple of years the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has travelled the country addressing the issue of high interest rates. He has talked a brave line, attacking the banks by suggesting that they are less than fair in their dealings with producers. That may be true in certain circumstances. Many farmers have found themselves locked into extremely high interest rates, and at the mercy of the banks. In order to consolidate previous debts, some of them assumed huge loans at interest rates of 19 or 20 per cent and, of course, have difficulty meeting the payments.
A measure such as this would be useful if it allowed the farmers to pay off their loans over a longer period of time at a more reasonable rate of interest. But the measure will not assist in that respect, Mr. Speaker, as it will probably only affect 1,000 farmers in the whole country. We should be dealing with a measure to help about 20,000 farmers. Available records indicate that the industry is in very serious difficulty, largely as a result of high interest rates, high input cost and depressed prices.
In the period January to October 1982, 344 farm bankruptcies were recorded, an increase of 50 per cent over 1981 and an increase of 87 per cent over 1980. I think we all recognize that this does not tell the whole story. It does not take into account those farmers who have abandoned their enterprise, liquidated their assets and moved on to other activities. It has been suggested that for every farmer who declares bankruptcy, ten others voluntarily leave the industry. If that is so, it is in very serious trouble.
Farmers have been caught in what I would call a devastating squeeze between high input costs and low product prices. The interest rate is but one component of the problem.
1 have to repeat, Mr. Speaker, that this is an insignificant, half-baked measure which will not solve the problem. It is but a superficial remedy. It is unfortunate that the 344 farmers who declared bankruptcy and the thousands of others who left the industry voluntarily, will probably never go back to farming. Many who were caught in the squeeze of borrowing money at high interest rates in order to consolidate their debts are now getting the runaround from the Farm Credit Corporation because of the limitation of this program which is being applied very strictly. Farm Credit Corporation officials have a firm set of guidelines and regulations to which they must adhere. They cannot extend help to borderline cases and, as a result, there is despair and frustration in the industry.
November 24, 1982

My colleague who spoke earlier mentioned the impact of all these things on young farmers and those just starting out. They could not have foreseen that interest rates would double within 12 months, and so, in good faith, they invested in equipment, stock and land. Based on a 10 per cent interest rate, their cash flow projections showed that they could have made a living from their enterprise, but now they are threatened. We have not been able to address their problems nor does this Bill address them adequately.
The vast majority of farmers who find themselves in trouble today will not qualify for help under this measure. 1 am sure that Hon. Members who represent rural ridings will have had the experience, day in and day out, of farmers coming to the constituency office for help with their problems.
Just the other day a farmer came into my office. He had an existing Farm Credit Corporation loan and was quite laudatory about the way the Corporation had dealt with him. Now, however, because he got sucked in to taking out a high interest loan at the bank, he needs to have his debts consolidated as he is barely making ends meet. This legislation is designed to give such farmers a breathing space, but unfortunately he does not qualify. This is a tragic situation, Mr. Speaker. All sorts of phony excuses are being given for the fact that he does not qualify. One is that he does not have enough experience. Mr. Speaker, he is a second or third generation farmer. His father homesteaded and his brothers are presently farming in the area. This young man needs a break to allow him to turn the operation into a viable enterprise.
While this legislation is a start, 1 would implore Hon. Members opposite to put pressure on the Minister of Agriculture and on the Cabinet to give more help to people who find themselves in difficult circumstances. While this Bill offers a measure of relief on interest rates it does not offer any help on prices.
I have said that this is a half-baked measure and that it is a sort of flim-flam, Mr. Speaker. I think the same thing could be said of the Small Business Incentives Program. Many businessmen have come to my office asking if the Program is in effect. They have been to the bank to inquire, but no application forms are available. There has been a lot of publicity to the effect that farmers and small-businessmen were going to get a break on interest rates, but this has not occured, Mr. Speaker. Under this measure, only 500 farmers will get any relief. I do not know how many people qualify under the Small Business Incentives Program but it is a drop in the bucket compared to the magnitude of the problem.
This Bill is a gesture, Mr. Speaker, but it certainly does not offer any genuine help to an industry in extreme need. We know that prices for agricultural products have been depressed while food prices have gone up by 8 per cent. Farmers are getting as much as 20 per cent less for their produce. I should like to refer to a headline which appeared in a newspaper in Vermilion, The Standard. It indicated that Prairie farm incomes would drop by 28 per cent, according to an assertion made by the United Grain Growers at their annual meeting. A 28 per cent drop in farm income in the current desperate
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
economic situation does not augur well. Agriculture is one of the basic and fundamental industries which needs support, not all the time but to get over the rough spots.
Wheat and feed grain prices are at a level where they provide roughly one-half of the purchasing power they provided in 1973-74 or roughly one-third of what they provided in 1970. There is not much that we can do in terms of market prices, in that much of our agricultural produce is sold on the export market. We are grateful that we have an export penetration of roughly $9 billion, but there is not much we can do because we have to compete with the subsidies and treasuries of other companies on international markets.
We must be efficient and productive. We must address the input side of the equation. This is something that can be done by Government because, in my view, Government is the biggest culprit in driving up farm input costs. The Government can do something about it. There is a raging debate about the freight rate situation, and I am very disturbed. Generally farmers recognize that they will probably have to pay more to move their grain to market positions. How much more is really the question. I should like to refer to an interview with the Chairman of the CNR which was reported in the November 18 edition of The Western Producer, wherein it was indicated:
-farmers should assume they will have to pay all freight cost increases above the annual Crow benefit payment guaranteed by the Government-
1 think this will really cause alarm in the farming community. As it now stands, the CNR Chairman is suggesting that farmers should not expect the Gilson formula to apply and that the Government of the day will meet the Crow gap, which is something in the order of $612 million or $644 million, depending upon the figure one wants to use. Also he is suggesting that producers will have to pick up the total of anything above that, but Gilson did not ask for that. The newspaper article went on to indicate:
He said he is skeptical of any Government assurances about obligations to future cost increases.
If the producers of Canada have to foot the bill for all additional increases of a freight rate structure with open-ended escalation, it will be a further drain upon them because they will not be able to pass that additional cost on to the consumers who purchase their grain. I am not sure whether the Chairman of the CNR was speaking on behalf of the Government or whether this is another manifestation of his rather dramatic conversion. At one time he was on the farmers' side of the issue; now he seems to be on the side of the railways. The Government of the day has some control and some ways and means to check that development.
Another area in which the Government could clearly act is the area of energy. The Government of Canada could do something rather significant in terms of ameliorating the situation with respect to energy. It is very clear that the federal Government is involved in a massive revenue grab in terms of the taxes it imposes upon all forms of energy, particularly fuel. Fuel and natural gas are major components

November 24, 1982
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act of the production of food in the country. The Minister of Agriculture goes about the country saying that the federal tax only accounts for roughly 20 percent of fuel costs, but 1 submit that that is grossly inaccurate and is another manifestation of the fraud and the flim-flam emanating from that side of the House.
I should like to refer to some of the per gallon components. I still use the term "gallon" because it is the one farmers use for comparison purposes. I see the minister who used to be responsible for things like metrication in the House this afternoon. He knows of what I speak and that the metric system in the farm community is not very popular. Bearing that in mind, I will use the term "gallon". When we look at the price of fuel in Canada at $1.56 per gallon, we find that 69 cents of it consists of federal tax. In the case of diesel fuel, for example, the 7 cent excise tax is not applicable, so that reduces it to 62 cents. If the Minister is talking simply about the federal sales tax, then he may be right, but I remind him that there is more than simply the federal sales tax. The excise tax on a per gallon basis is 7 cents. There is a 9 per cent federal sales tax which accounts for 15 cents per gallon. Then there is the petroleum compensation charge of 18 cents per gallon and the Canadian ownership charge-to buy Fina and British Petroleum which is also used to support the activities of Petro-Canada in Tanzania, Bangladesh, Jamaica and all over the world-which amounts to 4 cents per gallon. Also there is the petroleum and gas revenue tax, another federal tax which amounts to 7 cents per gallon, and when we look at the corporate tax of 24 per cent of $24.75, it works out to 18 cents per gallon, for a total of 69 cents per gallon. In the case of farm diesel fuel, it is reduced by some 7 cents.
In the last election campaign, the Minister of Agriculture promised special consideration for farmers so that they would not have the burden of huge federal sales taxes. There has been no relief at all for Canadian producers.
The situation is the same in terms of natural gas. This happens in the Minister's own backyard. The fact of the matter is that greenhouse operators are crippled by an exorbitant, devastating, confiscatory tax.
A good friend of the Minister, Nick Ingratta of Nick Ingratta Farms Ltd., 504 Seacliffe Drive West, Leamington, Ontario, said that in the early 1970s it was estimated that fuel costs were approximately 20 to 25 per cent of gross operational costs. Then he went on to point out the natural gas liquids tax of 68 cents per MCF and the Canadian ownership tax of 15 cents per MCF. But he overlooked another tax which works its way into the price, the petroleum and gas revenue tax of roughly 24 cents, for a total of $1.05 per MCF.
Of a total purchase of natural gas worth $75,000 in 1981, Mr. Ingratta's payment of the federal tax applicable was in excess of $20,000. This destroys the competitive edge. What is really ridiculous is that we are trying to promote and encourage the use of natural gas because it is in great supply in western Canada and it reduces our reliance upon imported
products. Simply, we have nothing more than a massive federal tax grab.
I will continue by referring to the Federation of Alberta Gas Co-ops. It is made up of 77 members, county-owned utilities and other private gas utilities in the Province of Alberta. They provide services to 140,000 rural people. A brief was presented to Members of Parliament. In this brief we find:
The Federation of Alberta Gas Co-ops objects to the Federal Natural Gas Excise Tax and will advise its members to pay this Tax under strong protest.
I think that summarizes the disaster that is inflicted not only upon farming industry but indeed on every industry. The brief continues:
The Natural Gas Excise Tax will:
(a)	impose a great deal of hardship on the less affluent members of our society
and those who can least afford it;
(b)	place a substantial increased financial burden on the Canadian farmer at a
time he can ill afford it;

(g)	generally adversely affect the Canadian economy.
This brief goes on to state that the natural gas excise tax must be repealed, and in the interval, pending its repeal, an extension of time for paying the tax must be granted. I think that summarizes the situation very well.
According to the Palliser Wheat Growers' Association's calculations, the tax on fuel oil and the tax component used for the manufacture of fertilizer works out to about $10 an acre. If you are farming a 1,500 acre farm, each farmer farming a farm that size is paying $15,000 into the federal Government coffers. There is certainly something which this Government could do about that. That is nothing more than a producer rip-off. The Minister comes along and attempts to placate the producers of Canada with this Bill. In my view, this Bill is only a gesture. It provides some aid and some temporary relief to
1,000	producers in Canada, but we should be dealing with something that will provide relief to more like 20,000 producers. What does the Minister do? He tries to sell us Cana-grex. He tries to sell the producers Canagrex so that the Government of the day can put its thumb on the pulse of all the farmers in this country.
This Minister supported a devastating budget, the one introduced last November, 1981. This budget proved to be disastrous, not only to the agricultural community but, indeed, to all sectors of Canadian society. The Minister of Agriculture could help producers now by prevailing on his Cabinet colleagues to reduce the federal Government take on energy, costs, on fertilizer and on all the components used by farmers in terms of energy and fertilizer. The Minister could certainly take action to remove those taxes which to me amount to outright confiscation.

subtopic: FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO REDUCE INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on Bill C-134, respecting rebates on interest on farm loans made under the Farm Credit Act. The legislation here today, the amendment to the Farm Credit Act, is to authorize the Farm Credit Corporation to offer some $200 million in loans, with the interest rate to be reduced by 4 per cent for two years. I support the intent of this Bill. It is something that has perhaps
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
come too little too late. There is much more the federal Government has to do in the area of agricultural financing. But I do support the intent of the legislation that we are dealing with today.
I want to talk about some of the problems 1 see in farm financing. I would like to make some suggestions that we in the New Democratic Party call improvements over what we have at the present time.
The problem for the Farm Credit Corporation is the formula which sets the rates for loans for a six-month period. These interest rates are locked in at present to 15.75 per cent. But money is available from other sources at 14 per cent or less. Having a discrepancy in interest charged on loans causes some problems. Farmers do not need any increase in their burden by way of higher interest rates from an institution that is supposed to be helping them.
I believe the Farm Credit Corporation sets its rates each year on October 1 and April 1. However, if a farmer borrows money from the Farm Credit Corporation he is locked into an interest rate for the entire term of the loan even if the interest rate six months down the road is significantly less on the market. For instance, if the rate is set at 15.75 per cent and the term for the loan is 20 years, that interest rate must be paid no matter whether the rate is reduced six months down the road by the FCC.
The Farm Credit Corporation has introduced a penalty, something that concerns me. If a loan is closed out before the end of a term, a penalty of three months' interest is charged. There are a few exceptions. On a loan of $100,000, a three-month penalty would cost a person about $4,000 to terminate the mortgage or the borrower's agreement with the FCC.
It is shameful of the federal Government to bring in that type of a penalty against farmers who are faced with very serious economic times at the present. It is ironic to find that a few months ago we were calling on the federal Government to put more money into the Farm Credit Corporation so that it would be able to expand the lending capacity of the Corporation, yet we find now that the situation exists where there are not very many farmers to whom loans are being given, and certainly no new loans. Farmers who wish to expand their operations or those who wish to start into farming do not want to go to the Farm Credit Corporation because money is so much cheaper through the private markets than it would be through the Corporation. Even if there were increased money in the Farm Credit Corporation right now, it would still be sitting there because the farmers do not want to borrow it and be penalized for dealing with a federal Crown corporation which was initially set up to be in the best interests of farmers themselves.
we are heading into a period of lower and lower net farm incomes as grain prices continue to decline on the world market and, meanwhile, costs such as those for energy, fertilizer and interest charges continue to increase for people involved

November 24, 1982
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
in the agricultural sector, in farming operations. In 1979 there were some 82 farm bankruptcies in Canada, and then, one year later, that number had doubled to 164 farm bankruptcies. In 1981, farm bankruptcies again increased to 191, and it is even worse this year. At this point in time we cannot know how many farm bankruptcies there will be over the entire year, but we do know that in the first three quarters of this year, some 316 family farms went into bankruptcy and that number could be much higher by the end of the year.
The Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), who spoke just before me, pointed out that this does not really give a true indication of the economic hardship which many family farms are going through right now, because there are some people who choose either to sell off their farming operations to farmers with larger operations in the area or, sometimes, to rent out their land and go out and find jobs on other farms so that they can subsidize their income in order that their families can have a decent level of income. Total farm incomes have changed very little from the 1974 level. In 1974, total farm incomes came to some $3.5 billion. In fact, this year total farm incomes will be less than the 1974 level. When we take inflation into account, it is fair to say that they would possibly be about one half of what they were in 1974.
The real problem of farm credit is not simply the problem of inadequate credit, which I have already tried to point out. There is more than enough credit available right now. It is not the right type of credit and it is not something which will help the farmers and those involved in farming in the long run. It is actually a problem of net incomes being too low to pay the bills and upgrade their operations in order to maintain viable farms. Farmers have actually borrowed increasing amounts. The borrowing rate has increased quite significantly. If we look back to 1970, we find that the accumulated farm debt in Canada was approximately $4.2 billion, and it had risen last year by almost four times to $16 billion, that being the total amount of debt farmers had gone into here in Canada.
Also, many Hon. Members have spoken in the House about some alternatives to what we have right now in the area of financing farming operations or putting together the necessary capital which farmers must have in order to continue. It is imperative that farmers have a line of relatively cheap or at least competitive credit that they can count on as being stable. One of the problems we find with the interst rates right now involves the insanity of the monetarist policies of allowing interest rates to fluctuate so wildly. When a farmer is going to put in his seed in the spring and he wants to borrow some money to continue his farming operation through until fall, it makes it very difficult for him, as it is for small business people and others who must rely on credit, to capitalize on his operation during the year and it is very difficlt for him to plan his budget on the farm. When the farmer does not know whether the interest rate will be 10 per cent or 25 per cent at the end of the year, it makes it very difficult for him to plan his year.
When we consider some of the other constructive suggestions which have been made and which should be followed, we should also consider the agri-bond concept which has been
mentioned by other Hon. Members in the House. The agribond concept is a good idea because it would provide a real pension plan for those farmers who do not usually contribute to a pension plan, many of them not at all. Many of the farmers in my own constituency whom I know personally rely upon the sale of their farms and farm assets at the end of their term of farming. Quite often they wish to turn their farms over to family members. They may sell to neighbours or to someone else, but over their lifetime they have really relied on building up their farming operations to provide for a dignified and decent retirement. Many farmers have sacrificed all their lives so that they can look forward to their retirement and a standard of living to which they have been accustomed. When a farmer sells his farm upon retirement now, he is quite often hit with a very heavy capital gains tax, and if there is one area in which the tax is unfair, I believe it is when it affects those who are involved in farming, those who have invested in their farms as their retirement package.
The agri-bond concept would be good if the Government were to see fit to put legislation into place which would allow farmers who have sold their farms for their retirement years to invest their money in a fund set up by the Farm Credit Corporation so that they could get relief and not pay capital gains on that amount. They would be returned an interest rate which might possibly be somewhat lower than the private market rate at that time. However, the rate that they would get on the capital gains for the bulk of the capital they had invested in the Farm Credit Corporation fund would certainly offset the lower interest rate they would be getting.
I think many farmers would be happy if they were able to invest in an agri-bond system set up through the Farm Credit Corporation, In turn, this would possibly provide the Farm Credit Corporation with a cheaper source of monay than its present source in the private market. I understand that the Corporation is thinking of floating $100 million in bonds on the United States market. The Corporation is in somewhat of a quandary right now because it is waiting until the interest rates reach the lowest possible point to try to pass that benefit on to the farming population of Canada, which wishes to take advantage of the Farm Credit Corporation loans, and we hope the rates will be coming down in the near future.
When farmers invest money in the Farm Credit Corporation it benefits them when they retire. It also benefits new farmers who are getting into farming and farmers already involved in the farming operation, because it gives them a supply of capital that they need to continue their farming operation, at a preferred rate.
One thing that I would like to touch on before I close off my remarks is the fact that an increasing number of farmers are feeling that they are being driven off their farms. This is true. It is indicated in the number of farm bankruptcies that we have had increasing very dramatically over the years, but it is also indicated in the hidden areas, such as when people have
November 24, 1982

either rented their farms out or they have almost turned into hobby farmers. They have sometimes sold off at a loss just to get out of the farming operation. This brings me to the area where I have real concern, that of people earning off-farm income. I can see why they earn off-farm income because many farmers, especially those on a smaller scale with a quarter section or possibly up to a section of land need that money to increase their family income to a large enough extent that they can keep on farming and keep some sort of decent lifestyle. I think that when farmers have to do this, the farming operation itself suffers. They are not spending the time that they should be.
We have to look at ways of stabilizing prices for farm products that will allow those involved in farming to plan over a longer period of time. The New Democratic Party over many years, and the CCF before them, have advocated orderly marketing. I agree with the orderly marketing concept. I believe it should be expanded in many areas of agriculture, but if there was another way, Mr. Speaker, that prices could be stabilized for people involved in farming throughout this country, whether it is potatoes in Prince Edward Island, fruit in British Columbia or wheat in Saskatchewan, I would agree with that, because farmers need a stable price for their products so they do not have to go off the farm and earn this extra income.
I am quite upset with Revenue Canada. They are connected with off-farm income as well. I have had several complaints recently from constituents whom I represent about Revenue Canada doing an audit on many farmers. I do not know whether they picked out one section of Saskatchewan or one section of Canada, but they have been doing several audits on people who have declared off-farm incomes. They have seen fit in many of these instances not to allow some of the regular farm deductions that would have normally been allowed in the past, and still should be allowed today because, although these are bona fide farmers and are in a full-time farming operation, they need the off-farm income to keep their operation going. I think it is a sad state of affairs when we find that we have farmers who have to neglect their business and then are punished even futher by the federal Government's not allowing them the deductions that they should have available to them as bona fide farmers.
I support the intent of Bill C-134 in that it does in fact give a two-year break to farmers who are getting money from the Farm Credit Corporation. It is lowering the amount for two years from 15.75 per cent to 11.75 per cent.
I have another reservation that I would like to bring out and that is that at the end of the two years the farmers who take advantage of the money from the Farm Credit Corporation under this new piece of legislation will find themselves locked in at 15.75 per cent when at that time the market rate may be much, much lower.
I would urge the federal Government to look at stabilizing farm prices for farm products. I would also ask them to be a little more sympathetic. I refer to the Departments and
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
agencies of the federal Government that do in fact deal with our farming population. In Saskatchewan and many other areas of Canada agriculture is the number one industry. The prosperity of many regions in Canada depends on agriculture.
I think if we continue to treat people of our farming communities in the way we have until now, we will find ourselves in the position where we are not producing sufficient food to fill our own requirements. We do not do that now in some areas, but it will get even worse in years to come.
I would also urge the federal Government and all Members of the Opposition to keep in mind that agriculture and transportation are vitally intertwined together. One cannot succeed very well without the other, especially in some of the landlocked Provinces where we have to go to more expensive methods of transporting agricultural products. We need the benefit of good transportation policies to get our products to the people who need them in other parts of Canada, and in other parts of the world.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the Hon. Members who have spoken before on the very important issue of farm credit, credit and financial assistance to farmers. speechtext:
As my colleague from Vegreville says, it is a mere pittance, and he described that very well in his remarks on this legislation, and I know that all Members of this House were listening very carefully.
The Minister, in the years that he has been Minister of Agriculture-and I have been here all those years-has done really very little for Canadian agriculture. The one thing that he has done and probably is doing today is that he has been the Minister of Agriculture who has travelled more than any other Minister in this country. He is constantly in the air, putting out fires here and there, instead of coming into this House with legislation to assist farmers and to allow them to operate and produce food not only for Canada but for many other countries in the world that need it. He is the PR man for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and for agriculture. He is not presenting to this House the kind of legislation or the kinds of ideas

November 24, 1982
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
that are necessary to assist a most important industry in this country.
Let us just look at what he has done in the last ten years. He has presented 13 bills to this House that have passed. Three of those bills have been in farm credit. Another bill has been in the farm improvement loans area. Most of the other bills, excepting one, have only been bills to update legislation that had been passed in the previous Parliaments. The only bill that is new has been the Bill for the Meat Import Act, an Act that was almost forced upon the Minister because of surpluses in other countries of the world coming into this nation. He has brought forward futuristic legislation to assist the farmers, something being proposed by Hon. Members in this House today. Why have we not seen legislation to reduce the farm fuel tax? That is very important legislation that could be passed quickly. It would greatly assist the farmers right across this country. It was earlier put on record that every farmer who farms in the neighbourhood of 1,000 acres is adding $1,500 to the federal coffers. Most western grain farms average 700 to 1,000 acres, as the previous speaker mentioned, and more and more farmers are being forced to rent their land. As a result, practising farmers are being offered so much land they cannot handle it. They are stretching their assets.
For the first time in many years farmers have to borrow from the banks the working capital in order to put in their crops. They cannot save enough money to put in a crop. If in some way their crop should fail, they have no other choice than to sell their assets or go bankrupt. That is the serious problem being faced not only by young farmers or those starting up but by established farmers as well.
Why has the Minister not talked to the western grain stabilization people with regard to getting the payment out early this year? Farmers are in desperate need of that money. There will be a payment this year and it ought to go out quickly. Members of this House and agricultural organizations across Canada have proposed that the advance payment be increased to $30,000, and $45,000 for corporate farms, from the present $15,000. For the average farm of 700 to 1,000 acres, $15,000 will not even pay the fertilizer bill. Therefore, that amount ought to be increased quickly. This is not new; it is an idea that people have been talking about.
The Minister of Agriculture should bring together his provincial counterparts. He should ask for their ideas with regard to stabilizing farm income. Every time the ministers attempt to get together, the Minister of Agriculture goes back to his old favourite, the marketing board. If it does not involve a marketing board, the Minister will not talk about stabilization. He favours the supply management marketing board. Most farmers do not want such an order from the Minister. They would rather talk about a program that does not involve such a board.
Many Members have said the Minister should look at new credit ideas. The agri-bond concept has been put forward by both opposition Parties and looked upon favourably by many
people as a way of getting Canadians to invest in a Canadian industry rather than outside the country. It could be done very easily with that concept.
There has been talk about the capital gains tax. Not only is it tough to pay the capital gains tax when selling out to retire, which few farmers can afford to do, but when a farmer is forced to sell his assets, not only must he meet his debts, but the Government is there with its hand out looking for a capital gains tax.
An excellent proposal was put forward by the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil). He is suggesting that those farmers who would have to pay capital gains tax when selling their assets be allowed to put that money into the Farm Credit Corporation at a low rate of interest. If the money is left in for a period of more than five years, when they receive that money back it would not be subject to capital gains tax. If this idea were adopted, loans could be made to farmers in desperate straits at lower interest rates. It would not only help 900 or 1,200 farmers, but it would help the 20,000 who are now in financial difficulty. This could be put into place immediately.
A previous speaker referred to off-farm income. Many farmers are forced to work outside their farms in order to get enough money to support their families. Their farm income is only enough to pay the debt. A lot of their income is invested in the farm in order to better it. The Government will not respond to the suggestion that we raise the $2,500 deduction as well as the additional $5,000 of which 50 per cent can be written off. This should be brought up to date. It has now been in place for ten years. Because many farmers are now forced into the off-farm income position, this amount should be increased.
For the past ten years this Minister has only been updating legislation. He should be putting into our embassies and trade commissions those who are knowledgeable in agriculture to assist us in our trade. For years we have been making that recommendation. Instead we get a Canagrex Bill with powers of extraordinary magnitude. This makes every farmer in the country shake in his boots. We should now have people in the trade houses looking for export markets for our farmers.
We need leadership to respond to situations such as that in the United States where there is a huge surplus of grain and oilseeds. With its large treasury, it has now put in place export credit packages. Because of these interest-forgiving packages, they will be capable of stealing our traditional markets.
A similar type of assistance could be given through our Canadian Commercial Corporation. It may not be necessary to do that in the same volume, but with the present recession many of our traditional customers require that kind of assistance. We ought to be there to ensure that these markets are not lost.
The largest portion of our imports are fruits and vegetables. We have the capacity in Canada to produce those vegetables and some fruits in our greenhouses. We not only have the capacity to produce, but this is a labour-intensive industry. At
November 24, 1982

this time of high unemployment, we ought to foster our greenhouse industry in every way possible.
We have a surplus of natural gas. However, the onerous tax on the natural gas is driving many greenhouse operations out of business. Farm credit will not assist them. It will not provide the loans they require to stay in business when the cost of fuel to heat the greenhouse has in some cases increased by 100 per cent per year. This creates an impossible situation.
The federal Government ought to assist in providing alternative systems of heat for greenhouses. Pumping stations all across the Prairies are emitting heat into a 20 below atmosphere. That wasted heat could be funnelled into the greenhouse industry at almost no cost. In addition to a tremendous amount of vegetables being produced, it would create thousands of jobs.
These are the types of ideas that we should be hearing from the Minister of Agriculture. Instead, we see amendments to a Farm Credit Bill that will only help 200 or 300 farmers. We are seeing amendments to bring up to date old pieces of legislation that were brought in by other Governments. subtopic: FARM LOANS INTEREST REBATE ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO REDUCE INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak in this debate on the amendments to the Farm Credit Corporation Act. Each day when Members stand to speak in the House, we hear time and again of the mills that are laying off shifts, of factories that are forced to close their doors and of small businesses that have been pushed into receivership. That causes us all a great deal of concern. I suspect that we on the opposition side are more concerned because one gets the distinct impression that the Government still does not recognize that there is a serious problem in the industrial sector of this country. One gets this impression based on the Government's actions and its proposed solutions. It is our hope that the Members on the Government side will realize how serious are the problems facing that sector and the fact that we are on the edge of an industrial collapse unless the Government takes some action. Let us hope and pray on a daily basis that the Government will see the challenge before it and take it up.
While we are all concerned about the demise of small businesses, medium businesses and the large corporations in our country, we begin to become very concerned when the agricultural sector faces real difficulties. Cattlemen, farmers, orchardists and so many others participating in food production in Canada are finding themselves in greater difficulty each day. Some very definite trends have been emerging which I consider to be dangerous. For example, the small family farm is falling by the wayside while the large corporate sector-the agri-business-is taking over the impetus in food production in Canada. Families who have lived on their land for many generations are being forced to move because they cannot meet
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
the high interest costs the Government has placed upon them. As well, farmers, cattlemen and others who have been on their land for generations are now forced to rent their properties to others because of the difficulty they have in marketing their goods.
A few months ago I had the good fortune to co-chair a task force on the economy which toured virtually every sector of each province. Farmers and food producers appeared before that task force to offer distinct solutions to their problems. They indicated that if they were given the opportunity and provided some encouragement by the federal Government, and the Provinces in some cases, they could double and perhaps triple or quadruple the amount of food they were producing. As was suggested by another Hon. Member who spoke recently, we are still importing fruits, vegetables and beef when the opposite could be true for many of these products.
We are faced with a grave situation. I would like to give some statistics which attempt in an objective, non-political and non-partisan way to describe accurately the situation as it relates to Canada's food production. In 1979 there were 82 farm bankruptcies in Canada. That number doubled one year later to 164 farm bankruptcies. In 1982 farm bankruptcies increased again to 191. The situation this year is even worse. While we only have the number of farm bankruptcies for the first three-quarters of this year, there already have been 316 family farms which have gone bankrupt. In the last nine months, 316 farmers could no longer make ends meet and were forced to shut down their operations. This situation should be considered totally unacceptable by Members in the House when we consider the vast agricultural resources and the potential capital and human resources which exist in our country. It is an outrageous situation.
I would like to speak for a moment about the farm situation in my Province of British Columbia. When one examines the struggle farmers in that Province are having, it presents a very bleak picture. The statistics on net farm income in British Columbia show that there was $136,458 million in terms of farm income in 1978. In 1979, that amount changed to $178,578 million. In 1980 that income began to decrease. In that year the net income for farm operations in British Columbia was $166,759 million. In 1981 it was reduced to $90,674 million. That represents a very serious decrease in income.
Let us consider the interest on indebtedness on British Columbia's farms. This statistic is something which all of us have become only too used to, that is, the matter of personal, business, corporate and farm indebtedness. In 1978, interest on indebtedness for B.C. farms totalled $62,524 million. In 1979 that had increased to $93,137 million. In 1980 it increased again to $116,437 million. In 1981 that figure skyrocketed to $189,873 million. These Figures illustrate the drastic increase in interest on indebtedness for B.C. farms in the last three years.
When one considers the outstanding farm debt in British Columbia, the statistics paint an even bleaker picture. In 1978

November 24, 1982

the outstanding farm debt was $956,079 million. This increased in 1979 to $1,163,093 million. In 1980 it had increased to $1,312,480 million. Unfortunately, the statistics for 1981 are not available but by all indications the outstanding farm debt will be well over $1,500,000 million. No matter what statistic one wishes to consider when trying to understand what is happening to farm incomes in Canada, it points to a very definite downward trend.
I would like to discuss the question of fertilizer costs and energy costs. These two areas are of special importance because these costs are beginning to skyrocket rather than decline.
For this example, Mr. Speaker, I want to turn to the great grain producing Province of Saskatchewan where energy and fertilizer costs are perhaps more important than in other areas. Over the last four-year period energy costs, including petroleum products, have risen substantially. In 1978 it was $171 million. In 1979 it had increased to $189 million. In 1980 it went up again to $215 million. In 1981 the figure had nearly reached $285 million.
So one can see, just by looking at these raw statistics, the incredible costs food producers are forced to bear as a result of increased fuel and energy costs. The tragedy, Mr. Speaker, is that these increases are the direct result of this Government's energy policies. It is a very sad day for the food producers of this country when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) week after week refuses to recognize the skyrocketing costs, and fails to take any action to ease the burden.
Let us turn for a moment to another area of cost which is perhaps even more important than energy, that of fertilizers. The fertilizer industry, because of its great dependence on energy, has seen fantastic increases in the cost of its product. That, of course, is directly related to the cost of food production. Again, let us objectively examine the increase in fertilizer costs over just the last four or five years. In 1978 the cost of fertilizer application in Saskatchewan was $101 million. In 1979 it had increased to $143 million. In 1980 it had gone up to $166 million. Then came the big jump in 1981 up to $205 million, and in 1982 to nearly $250 million.
On the one hand, Mr. Speaker, we see these increases in these two critical areas of energy and fertilizer, and on the other, the cost of seeds, barbed wire, building materials and equipment is increasing as a result of the inflationary problem we find ourselves in, and that is attributed directly to present Government policies. At the same time as these costs are increasing so dramatically, farm income in many cases has actually decreased. Looking at the price per pound that beef producers in central British Colombia receive, it has largely levelled out for the last number of years. In no way does it begin to match the rising costs of raising beef. If it were not for the beef stabilization plan in British Columbia, more accurately described as the Farm Income Assurance Plan, the small beef producers in British Columbia would not be in operation today. We can thank the New Democratic Party for the plan. When they were in power in British Columbia they
recognized the value of keeping the small family ranch in place and introduced that measure to preserve this very traditional part of the British Columbia and western Canadian landscape.
Over the last five years, Mr. Speaker, the cost to food producers of energy and fertilizer has increased by just under 80 per cent. Is it any wonder that people who are very knowledgeable about the food producers of Canada and the problems they face stand up and declare that many in this sector are on the edge of financial collapse? When you consider these few figures which I have just put before the House this afternoon, is it any wonder? Consider the most recent amendments to the legislation dealing with the Farm Credit Corporation, such as the one a few months ago which resulted in assistance to approximately 900 farm operators in Canada. Assuming that this Bill we are dealing with now is passed soon, it will provide relief to somewhere between 300 and 500 farmers. But we are just beginning to touch the surface of the problem, Mr. Speaker. The Government is not addressing the serious problems facing the food producers of this country.
There is a crisis in the grain industry, in the oil seeds industry, and a crisis in the beef industry in Canada. Nothing short of calling it a crisis would be appropriate, Mr. Speaker. Yet what is the Minister of Agriculture doing? Oh, we see him almost on a daily basis wearing his green hat and western boots. He likes to travel around the country visiting every single fair and every little agricultural meeting that he possibly can, telling everyone how hard he is working. Yet we in this House wait day after day to see a Bill which is going to provide assistance to food producers in Canada. The Minister reminds me of a snake oil salesman. He is a great showman with a lot of rhetoric, but unfortunately no action. The patience of food producers in Canada is beginning to wear a little thin. They like this man, they got the impression over the years that he has worked very hard for the farmers of this country. To pay respect where it is due, in many areas he has done a number of things to assist the food producers. But we are in a crisis today and it requires imagination, courage and a sense of creativity, which this present Minister of Agriculture simply does not have.
