Mr. Speaker, the hog producers in Canada are struggling this very day to survive. They see little light on the horizon in the way of help coming their way. What does the Minister do? He brings in an amendment to the Farm Credit Corporation which is going to provide a 4 per cent decrease in interest rates. He does not address the serious problem which faces the Corporation. Here is a Corporation which is intended to assist the farm community and which sets its rates every six months, I believe on April 1 and on October 1, and at the moment that Corporation has its rates locked in at 15.75 per cent. The interesting thing is that I can remember not many weeks ago when Members of the Opposition were having to stand up and literally plead and beg the Minister to increase the cash available to the FCC in order to meet the needs of the
November 24, 1982

food producers in Canada. Now, Mr. Speaker, you cannot give that money away. Because of a recent amendment to the FCC, that Corporation is now able to go out into the private money market, but to date no bond issue has been quoted because they have no need for the money. Interest rates are coming down so that now rather than borrowing from the FCC at 15.75 per cent, you can go out to the open private market and pick up money for 14 per cent, in some cases even less. What becomes abundantly clear is that the present interest rate formula of the Farm Credit Corporation is not working, particularly during the present unstable period.
The Government seems quite prepared to let the interest rate roller coaster go up one Thursday and go down the next Thursday, until it has become like a game. People wait until Thursday to see what the interest rate will be before making an investment. How can a food producer attempt to plan his operations when he has no idea what the interest rate will be in the days ahead? Any individual or businessman has a difficult time planning for the future when the interest rate can vary on a weekly basis.
Surely the Government could have done a favour to every business and individual by attempting to stabilize interest rates for at least six months. That is what it did with the Farm Credit Corporation. It said, "Despite the volatility in interest rates we will lock the Farm Credit Corporation rate for six months." That is of some assistance to food producers while interest rates increase. But if they drop below the six-month rate, then people working for the Farm Credit Corporation will have a long, leisurely winter, waiting for business which is going to the banks, the credit unions or other funding agencies.
The situation is a tragic one, Mr. Speaker. Yet the Minister of Agriculture masquerades as a snake oil salesman, travelling the country in an attempt to convince people that everything is all right.
Last weekend 1 had the sad experience of sitting down with a cattle producer who has a small, 200 head, operation in my constituency. He is now in his mid-30s and had grown up on a cattle ranch in central British Columbia, as had his father and his father before him. Raising cattle is the only thing this young man understands, and he is good at it. His wife and two children help him with the operation. He had difficulty obtaining much money from the Farm Credit Corporation so he borrowed $90,000 from the bank in order to get through the year. His interest payment is in excess of $15,000. He works full time, his wife works full time and his two teenage children work after school and on weekends. He is a man of strong character and he and his family have worked for the last four or five years to make this operation viable. Interest rates have made it imposible for him to continue, however. He and his family will have to walk away, after selling the ranch at a fire-sale price to a Swiss investor.
The implications of this case are tragic for Canada, Mr. Speaker. This man has lost faith in the country. He has long since lost faith in the Government and in its agricultural

policy. He has lost hope because of the way the Government has allowed the banks, in particular, to run roughshod over the food producers. Now he will have to try to find employment in the forest or mining industry in British Columbia, both of which are on their knees. It is a story of failure, after three generations in the livestock business in western Canada. He is no longer able to continue because of the policies of the Liberal Government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest as a voice from the Liberal benches called out that if I do not have anything good to say about the food industry, I should sit down. I will not sit down, Mr. Speaker. I will draw attention to the Government's lack of leadership and its inability to deal effectively with the lending institutions in the country in the last two years. There is no chance that I will just sit down and keep quiet and let the Government continue in this way.
The agricultural policies of the Government are at the root of the increasing number of farm bankruptcies in the country. Until the late sixties most of the long term credit needed by Canadian farmers was supplied by the Farm Credit Corporation, as well as much of the short-term and intermediate term financing needed by farmers. Then the Government began restraining the amount of credit the Corporation could provide to food producers. Chartered banks were invited into the farm credit market. In 1975, 72 per cent of all long-term credit taken out by farmers came from the Farm Credit Corporation. That made sense; it was designed to provide long-term funding to food producers. By 1979 only 35 per cent of farmers were able to meet their long-term credit needs with the fixed interest loans provided by the Corporation.
The Government, with its tight purse strings, has hamstrung the Farm Credit Corporation. It has prevented it from keeping up with the increasing demand for farm credit. In effect, it offered the banks, with their floating interest rates, a bigger piece of the farm credit action on a silver platter.
At the same time that it was knocking the props out from under the Farm Credit Corporation, the Government introduced drastic changes in its grain policy. Prior to the so-called open market, most feed grains had been marketed outside the Prairies under the auspices of the Canadian Wheat Board. Prices were relatively stable at that time, and the competitive capabilities of different regions of the country were more or less equal. But the Government's decision to move to the open market and to allow large grain merchants and feed mills back into the grain market on a nation-wide basis, upset the apple cart. The result was the transfer of some sectors of agricultural activity to different regions of the country. To aid that transfer, some provincial Governments got into the act with subsidized credit or out-and-out subsidies. By the end of the decade, much of the hog population had moved out of the Prairies into Ontario, Quebec and, to a lesser extent, the Maritimes. To a greater extent, cattle which originated in the Prairies were

November 24, 1982
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
being fed in eastern feed lots where the price of feed grain gave the producers a competitive advantage.
This must have looked very appealing to the Government economists because, with all the activity, it looked as though agriculture was booming. But, as I said, what was really happening was that production was shifting from one region of the country to the other, largely financed with borrowed money. It was fortunate that while this was happening there was a surge in grain prices that carried most farmers through to the end of the last decade. But with accumulated farm debt around $16 billion, and farm income now falling, as my earlier statistics demonstrated, the results of the shift in the Government's agri-food policy is becoming evident. Large investments were made in some parts of the country and abandoned in others. Farmers were forced to borrow greater amounts when interest rates were increasing at unprecedented levels. The total was $1.7 billion in 1981. In the early 1970s, credit costs ranked about eight or ten in the production costs of farmers. Now the cost of credit is the highest one facing Canadian farmers. While farmers were borrowing in greater amounts, the Farm Credit Corporation was prevented by the Government from keeping up with the demand for farm credit. Longterm credit at fixed rates was becoming less and less available.
Agriculture in Canada is in desperate straits today. With the Government's record of destabilizing policy changes and the reduction of farm credit interest rates by 4 per cent, it can only be considered a rather feeble attempt to deal with a very grave problem.
In the West things are done in more traditional ways when it comes to production. The people of western Canada have come to depend upon the institutions which provide security for the maintenance of those traditions, institutions such as the Crow rate and the Farm Credit Corporation.
The Farm Credit Corporation is the only agency which offers long-term Fixed interest loans to farmers. FCC loans can now be obtained at 15.75 per cent interest, but the floating rate available from banks or credit unions is for the time being lower than 15.75 per cent. Unless the formula now used to set FCC interest rates is changed, permitting the Corporation to lend at less than 15.75 per cent and to obtain funds at a lower rate, much of its fixed interest credit may go unused this year as farmers cash in on the temporary reduction in interest rate from commercial lending institutions. Already the Provinces are being pressured to move into the subsidization of farm credit. We could soon see a patchwork of subsidization programs which again stimulate production shifts from one region of the country to another, giving the illusion of a productive, vibrant farm industry, when in fact nothing could be further from the truth.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture has recommended time and time again the introduction of an agri-bond program similar to the small business bond. Under this proposal the Government would give FCC authority to borrow short-term, three to five years, by the issue of financial instruments on
which the interest is tax free. This money would then be lent to farmers requiring money at lower interest rates, not only for debt consolidation but also for essential investment and, more important, working capital. This is a proposal which could and should be introduced quickly. I would submit that it is a more rational and long-term solution to the farm credit crisis than the 4 per cent interest rate reduction which will be granted as a result of this Bill to benefit at best not more than a few hundred farmers.
If we are to have any stability in the Canadian agriculture industry, the Farm Credit Corporation must be expanded to provide enough long-term credit to service the bulk of farm credit needs across Canada. It needs to be expanded as well to provide short and medium-term credit in special cases. I am thinking of special cases where FCC credit can help a new farmer or new cattleman get started. But simply expanding the FCC is not enough to bring needed stability back to Canadian agriculture and to stimulate increased production. We in this Party have long supported the concept of stabilization programs. If stabilization programs are provided on a federal basis, and if marketing systems are in place which provide some equity across the country, Canadian farmers would be more confident that they will be able to get their costs of production, plus a decent standard of living off their land.
Bill C-134, to provide a 4 per cent interest rate relief, will provide only a very short-term solution to a serious problem. As I said earlier, it will help a few hundred farmers in grave financial difficulty who are crying out for relief from high interest rates. This proposal just begins to scratch the service of the farm credit crisis in Canada.
The FCC would be playing much more of a leadership role in terms of supporting the cutting edge of a thoughtful and dynamic industrial strategy for the food producing sector of Canada, if one were in place. The time has come for the Government of Canada to look at this critical industry, and industry which is critical in virtually every region of Canada; to identify those areas which need to be nurtured, encouraged and supported by the senior levels of Government, and to take steps to see that that is done. Canada is still required to import vast amounts of fresh vegetables, mutton, lamb and beef. This is totally unnecessary in a country such as ours with its vast potential.
The Government should take the leadership. We on this side of the House would be pleased to rally around and embrace a strategy in agriculture which makes sense and encourages Canadians to recognize the need to support a strong agricultural component in our economy. We should say to Canadians that perhaps for one morning a week they should drink apple juice rather than orange or grapefruit juice. That would mean 24 million people lifting glasses of apple juice. Think of what it would do for the orchards in British Columbia, central Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Suddenly there would be an instant demand for tens and perhaps even hundreds of new apple orchards overnight. If we could convince every person in the country to drink an extra glass of Canadian wine, think of

November 24, 1982

what it would do to the vineyard industry. We could go on and on; just by modifying our dietary and purchasing habits, we could provide a much needed stimulus and instant demand for many Canadian food producers. But, no, we live glibly on in a sort of continentalist mentality which has virtually become the catch word of the Liberal Government of Canada. One almost gets the impression that it does not want to encourage this critical sector or the family operation on the land.
It would appear by this Government's policy that corporate agriculture is the route to go. I am not suggesting that in selected areas it is not the route to go; in some cases corporate agriculture makes sense. But in many areas much more could be done to assist the family operation. Think of what it would do to the mood in the country if every Canadian was convinced that the food producing strategy of the Government would make sense in all regions. The people of Canada would rally around it and provide the necessary support.
I come from a part of Canada in central British Columbia which is not famous for its agricultural production, but to this day a number of people are still able to manage as food producers. I remember as a youngster, not many years ago, coming to that area and seeing vast acreages of potatoes, asparagus and tomatoes, vast areas of crabapple orchards, huge flocks of sheep, 5,000 ewes in a single flock, and herds of cattle in the neighbourhood of two or three thousand head. Now that is virtually all gone. They thrived in that particular environment for decades. Obviously the basis of the industry is there, but because of the lack of marketing procedures and credit opportunities, the farm and ranch industry has virtually deteriorated over the last two or three decades into at best a marginal industry today.
It is important for Members of the House, especially Hon. Members opposite, to know that this potential exists in Canada today. That opportunity is still in place. With the availability of energy in terms of coal, natural gas and geothermal energy, and with the waste heat of many large factories and mills, we could be producing much more.
In closing, let me say the opportunities are there. What we need now is a Government with the strategy to put the agricultural community back on the rails and to provide the support and encouragement to get that vital component of our economy going once again.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we are discussing third reading of Bill C-134. This is an important Bill. It deals with the farming community and the most important aspect of the farming community, which is finance. Finance is important today because we know that agriculture is no different than any other business in this country and that many businesses are experiencing financial difficulty.
Before I get to my main remarks on the Bill, I would like to pay tribute to my colleague, the late Hon. Member for Bran-don-Souris who passed away last week and whose funeral I
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
attended in Brandon yesterday. I did not have the chance to know the Honourable Mr. Dinsdale for a great number of years, but it was a privilege for me to sit with him in the House and be able to refer to him as a colleague. He was a great help to me as a new Member. I know he has been a great help to many others in this House. Mr. Dinsdale was the kind of man who, in my opinion, was an example of what a Canadian should be. He was a man of high principle, of high morals, and displayed it without a lot of flamboyance. Unfortunately, many of us do not realize what a Canadian is. In many ways Mr. Dinsdale exemplified what my idea of a Canadian should be. We will all sorely miss him, particularly those of us from Manitoba. It is true that you do not know how much you miss somebody until they are gone. That is the case with Mr. Dinsdale. I know some tributes were paid to Mr. Dinsdale in the House on Monday. Unfortunately, I was unable to be here because I was in my riding. I did, however, attend his funeral in Brandon yesterday. I just wanted to say a few words today about our dear colleague from Brandon-Souris.
The Bill before us is very important. Agriculture, like many other businesses, is in a considerable amount of trouble. We know there are something like 320,000 or 330,000 farms in Ontario. I have seen estimates that place the number of farms in trouble as high as 32,000 or 33,000, or ten per cent of the total. That is a large percentage; the number is large in terms of absolute numbers. These are farmers who have financial problems which could put them out of business.
This situation has serious implications for consumers. If farmers are forced out of business we know that one or two years, down the road less food will be produced, which means the cost will go up, causing rising inflation. It is in everybody's interest to keep as many farmers in production in this country. Not only is the farming community interested, everybody else has a large stake in it, too.
This Bill proposes to spend an additional $100 million. The $200 million mentioned in the bill is arrived at by taking $100 million out of the normal allocation that the Farm Credit Corporation has. The extra $100 million is made up of $16 million, which the Government has found to pay in direct interest assistance to lower interest rates for farmers, plus an additional $84 million in loans. When one talks about the $200 million figure, one has to bear in mind how the Government got to this $200 million. It is $100 million of old money and $100 million of new money.
We have to give the Government credit for that because it recognized the problem and it did find some additional money with which to address it. Our concern is not so much that the Government recognizes the problem, but that the Government waited so long and has been delinquent in acting. In many ways the Government has been contributing to the problem by allowing it to develop.
The $16 million that will be available in direct grants to farmers to lower interst rates works out to an average of about $50 per farmer in this country. We know that is not a lot of money when you put it in perspective. We are not saying we
20958

Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
are ungrateful for the $16 million, nor are we saying it will not be well used. I simply want to point our that $16 million spread among approximately 320,000 farmers works out to an average of $50 per farmer.
One must take into account that in many areas of the country it costs a farmer $100 to $200 to fill up the fuel tank on his tractor enabling him to work in the field for a day, that is twice or three times the $50. If a farmer buys a tonne of phosphorous fertilizer, it will cost him something like $300. That gives Hon. Members an idea of just how much assistance this $50 will be to him. Fifty dollars will not even buy a tonne of phosphate fertilizer. It will not go very far in terms of helping a farmer put his crop in, even as far as fuel expenses are concerned.
Because the amount of money available is so small, the total number of applicants will exceed by far the amount of money the Bill will make available for farmers. By taking $100 million out of the normal allocation of funds which the Farm Credit Corporation has, it will mean there will be $100 million less available to be loaned under the normal operations of the Farm Credit Corporation. That is of concern to us.
I want to talk specifically about interest rates. We know that the Farm Credit Corporation sets interest rates every six months. We also know that the rate set now is 15.75 per cent. Most people know that the prime rate is considerably lower than that today. Therefore, farmers who are locked into a Farm Credit Corporation loan are paying 15.75 per cent interest, a higher rate than if they were to go now and apply for a loan at a bank. I am not suggesting that farmers should be able to have it both ways; that is, a cheaper rate of interest when prime rates go up. In other words, farmers should not be able to get loans of 15.75 per cent interest when the interest rate at the bank is either at 17 per cent or 18 per cent. When the bank rate drops those people with Farm Credit Corporation loans should not immediately be released from those loans to go to the bank to receive a cheaper rate of interest for their loans, but I suggest that the Government and the Farm Credit Corporation give serious consideration in respect of those producers who have some problems paying the 15.75 per cent interest. That high rate of interest relative to today's prime is causing farmers financial problems. I know of one such instance in my own constituency about which I had some discussion this afternoon. In this particular case, if the producer were able to go to the bank and get a loan at the lower rate offered by the bank today it would make a significant difference, enabling him to stay in business.
1 would suggest the Minister and the officials in the Farm Credit Corporation give serious consideration regarding those farmers who are in trouble as a result of paying the 15.75 per cent interest rate. I would suggest the Minister and the officials consider releasing those farmers from that interest rate. I do not think that is asking a lot.
I understand the Government is considering changing the setting of the rates under the Farm Credit Corporation from every six months to perhaps every three or four months. There is nothing wrong with that. After all, when we are in fluctuating capital markets with interest rates going up and down quite
quickly, I do not think there is anything wrong with the Government considering adjusting interest rates sooner than every six months, which is what has been done up until now.
All of us have another concern which has been expressed by Members of the New Democratic Party and those of us in the Official Opposition. This Bill is a manifestation of the lack of leadership which this Government and, in particular, which this Minister have shown in the agricultural field over the past ten years. I understand the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) will, within the next week or ten days, be celebrating his tenth anniversary of being appointed the Minister of Agriculture. I am not sure that the farmers will want to celebrate when they think about this Minister having been at the helm of Canadian agriculture for ten years.
I submit that the agricultural industry is a very proud industry, and would much rather earn its own way than have to go to the Government for handouts and subsidies. However, if one considers the ten years that the present Minister has been in this position, one finds a very sad, lamentable and actually terrible testimony to what he has been able to accomplish. He has really taken a once proud industry and reduced it to an industry which is fighting amongst itself. It is looking inward for markets instead of being outward-looking-instead of looking to markets outside our country which would earn foreign exchange for our country and help us fight a lower Canadian dollar and hold down interest rates. Instead of doing that, he refers to marketing boards, saying to close the border and produce for a small market at home.
The Hon. Member from British Columbia who just spoke talked about producing all kinds of fruits and vegetables in this country, including some of the off-season fruits. I suggest that he must carefully consider the matter because,for instance, it would be very difficult to produce bananas and pineapples in this country. A certain amount of peanuts are grown in southern Ontario. However, we should be considering what we grow best; that is, whether we grow grain, beef, or pork best. If we are good at producing these products, and are capable of being competitive, we should be exchanging them for some of those others. I would rather see that kind of industry than one which looks to the Government for subsidies. That would be a much healthier situation for the farming community and for the total Canadian economy.
I would briefly like to refer to some of the things the federal Government and the Minister could and should be doing. These are not new, but have been mentioned in the House by other Hon. Members. In the past two or three years I have had the opportunity to mention them, but nothing seems to have happened. What we should first do in terms of western agriculture is to consider the Western Grains Stabilization Fund. First, we do not know whether there will be a payment this year. If there is to be a payment, we do not know how much it will be. I would submit that there is no reason that the level of payment, if any, could not be immediately announced to the
November 24, 1982

farming community. 1 am not suggesting that the payment be made, although that would be even better, but if the farmers at least knew that they would be getting something and when it would come, it would help them to budget and handle their cash flow. However, as it is, we know that we contribute one dollar for every $2 contributed by the federal Government. We think that is great, but we do not know when and if there will be a payment, or how much it will be. That is a very simple matter which would not take much extra organization or expertise on behalf of the Government, yet it would greatly assist farmers in terms of their cash flow.
We have suggested another item which could be considered, the second item, if you will. There should be an increase in the Advance Payments Act, which I believe has been in place since 1957. It was mentioned in this debate by the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger). It is an excellent suggestion. We have offered the Government that if it were to bring forth the amendment we would put it through very quickly.
This Program has been in operation since 1957 and has worked very well. It is simply a provision whereby the Government advances money to producers against the delivery of their own grain. Then, when the producer sells the grain, he pays a portion back to the Government and the Government picks up the interest. Admittedly, there would be a small additional cost to the federal treasury, but I submit that if one considers the additional money which would be gained from taxation, in many cases the additional cost would be offset against the quicker generation of revenue as a result of the additional money put in the hands of the producer. It is not a Government handout. It is simply an advance against some of the farmers' own money. This Program has worked well. It is outdated now because the limits are too low. An increase must be considered.
The third suggestion, as mentioned by the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), is that we need to consider the tax on farm fuel collected by the federal Government. I have in my hand a chart, and I will refer to my own Province of Manitoba. On a gallon of gasoline, the federal Government charges approximately 65 cents. It seems to me that in the interest of keeping farmers in business and food costs down, the Government could consider increasing the 7 cent a gallon excise tax rebate which is presently returned to farmers. That is another bone of contention. Rather than the Government collecting it all and then refunding it, there should be a provision in place whereby the producer should not have to pay it in the first place. This should apply not only to farmers but to the business community as well. As it is now, one pays it and then applies for a refund every six months, or whenever the amount of refund exceeds $200. I see no reason for the extra paperwork required of the business and farming community, as well as the Government, in simply collecting the money and then refunding it. If it is to be refunded, why not stop the practice of collecting it in the first place? That makes sense. Unfortunately, many suggestions we make in the House do make sense, but they are never listened to or acted upon.

Another item we could discuss ad infinitum involves capital gains. We should allow farmers to earn their way and generate money so they do not have to depend on Bill C-134 for a few Mickey Mouse handouts-a few dollars here and there.
We should also be able to expect a federal Minister of Agriculture to be truly a federal Minister. He should be willing and able to show some initiative in working with his provincial counterparts. The present Minister has done exactly the opposite. I know of a meeting which took place in Regina last spring attended by the representatives of provincial ministers of agriculture who sat down to discuss national stabilization programs for beef and pork. I know that the Minister responsible for DREE in this House had a more senior representative at that meeting than did the Minister of Agriculture. That is a disgrace. Surely, when we have a federal Minister of Agriculture, he should have enough common sense to act like a federal Minister and show some initiative, rather than being a hindrance, if anything.
We also know that approximately two weeks ago there was another meeting of provincial Ministers of Agriculture who, in principle, agreed on a national stabilization program for beef. It included all three parties and, by that, I mean the federal Government, the provincial Government and the producers. Our federal Minister of Agriculture was not there. 1 should not say "our", because I do not want to claim him as mine. However, the Minister of Agriculture who represents Canadian agriculture was not there. Again, to my mind, that is a disgrace.
Instead of having Canadian producers united, working together and being competitive with producers in other countries, like the United States, the European Economic Community, Argentina and Australia, so that Canadian agriculture can be competitive with them, what we end up with is a bunch of provinces stepping in, because of the lack of initiative by the federal Government, stabilizing their own red meat industries, causing provinces to bid against provinces. In effect, the result is Canadian farmers fighting amongst themselves for a share of the market, instead of being shown some leadership by a federal Minister so that they could all unite and be more competitive on the world scene. That has been the result of the Minister's ten years in office. It is sad testimony to what he has done in that ministry.
Another example of what we could do if we had some support from a federal Minister of Agriculture who had some brains, or who cared, is deal with the Americans; the American legislators, Congressmen and Senators, who are more than willing and are looking for us. It is our turn to sit down and discuss the world grain trade. We are not necessarily referring to a cartel. We should simply get together to hold some discussions on where world grain prices are going so that we can better understand the positions of the Americans, and they can understand ours. Simply put, it means that we would have legislators, elected people on both sides of the border, sitting down and holding discussions.
There was such a meeting a year ago in Washington. It is now Canada's turn to host a meeting this year, but to date we

Not much may come of them, but if we could at least have the chance to sit down on a formal basis and carry on discussions with the Americans, I think we would realize that we both have the same problems, and we may reach some common ground from which we could go forward to firm up grain prices. We all know that some grain prices are $1 a bushel lower than a year ago, even though our cost of production is continually rising.
Another example of how the Government and the Minister have failed to help farmers generate income can be found by considering what has happened with the levy under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. A good point, it more than could have doubled; it probably could have tripled. We want some support from this Government. We do not necessarily want handouts. We want some support so we can earn our way and get ourselves in a position where we do not have to borrow money and come back to the Government and look for these kind of Mickey Mouse programs, to adjust a program or adjust a Bill and give a few dollars to this farmer and a few to that.
Another area on the international sphere that I feel very strongly about is that Canada has been very badly represented at any of the international negotiations that go on with regard to tariffs. There are negotiations going on currently in Geneva concerning some of the problems of the GATT agreement. We know that the European Economic Community has managed so far to keep most of their agricultural products out of the jurisdiction of the GATT. I think that is totally wrong. If we had a Minister and had a Government that really understood
some of the things that the agricultural industry is capable of doing for this country and this economy they would take those negotiations more seriously and see that Canadian agriculture is given a fair chance to compete on some of the world markets. That goes for Japan as well. We are not asking for favoured treatment but we are asking for at least a chance to compete fairly for those markets. If any of those people are watching or listening to me, they will know that in many cases the European Economic Community and Japan are not necessarily fair players when it comes to agricultural commodities. They are very good at keeping our products out, with both tariff and non-tariff barriers.
Let me say a little bit about how I think we differ from the NDP and what their policies would be. The farming community in this country is in many cases very young. In western Canada it is not much older than 100 years, and in some cases it is less than that. It has got to be where it is, I know it has been very successful and in many cases it has been very prosperous, because it has relied on individual initiative to create that wealth, and it has rewarded the individual for doing that.
The NDP, I believe, having listened to some of their speeches and followed some of their programs, think that everything should be run from the centre and that largely Government programs should control everything, and we know what that means. It means administering programs from the centre and not giving the incentive and reward to the individual producer who takes the risk. That is how we differ. If you look at history you will realize that this country was settled by individual homesteaders who took some initiative on their own. It was not settled by a horde of bureaucrats from Ottawa going out and saying, "You chop down a tree and you work after supper and you sacrifice on behalf of your family so that you can have a better piece of farmland". That is exactly the wrong way to create wealth in this country, and that is exactly the kind of policies that the NDP are advocating by supporting these measures that the Minister of Agriculture has brought forward, like Bill C-134. That is exactly the kind of thing this present Government is supporting.
I would suggest there is no reason why we should not support the Bill. It seems to me that if we do not support the Bill we would be a lot more irresponsible than the present Minister, and Lord only knows how irresponsible he is toward Canadian agriculture. I would suggest that Canadian agriculture would be a lot better served by programs that could be developed by a Government and a Minister that understood agriculture, cared about it and saw that it was productive so it could pay its own way, not have to borrow as much money and, therefore, have to rely on Mickey Mouse Bills like Bill C-134.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am very happy to be able to speak for a few moments on Bill C-134, a Bill to provide rebates under the Farm Credit Corporation Act.
When the farms do well in this country, as in other countries in the world, then the whole country does well. That has been
November 24, 1982

an accepted fact with most Governments across the world, and most Governments take into consideration that if you help the farmer to be secure, to be able to make a living, to make enough from his production to stay alive, to help his family, then your whole country can be prosperous.
The basis of the affluence of Canada is the agricultural industry, and it is very important that we keep that industry able to provide the kind of continued direction that it has had in the past.
The speaker just before me suggested that our Party's position was not based on the farmers doing what they can to produce and continue to produce food for the world, but no farming industry can be built on the kind of policies that have been put forward by this Government. Those have led to continued bankruptcies or farmers having to sell out and leaving the industry to the consolidation, to the extent where the industry is becoming weaker and weaker.
If we believe that the agricultural industry is a basic industry in this country then we in this House should be doing something about it. We should be doing all we possibly can to make the industry secure. This Bill is a very small attempt to do something to keep the farmer afloat. What we should be doing is making the industry secure.
The agricultural industry in Canada at the present time has a $22 billion debt. About $2 billion per year is being taken out of that industry to finance that debt. This is the highest level of debt that the industry has ever had, even if you take into consideration the inflation of the dollar. That is a very interesting statistic because what we are really saying is that there is something so badly wrong with this industry that the debt is increasing as we go along. Instead of an industry which pays off its debt and allows the people involved in it to be affluent and to make a living to pay for the production of their goods, we are getting further and further into debt.
The reason for this is fairly obvious. Last year the income of the agricultural industry across Canada was reduced by about 17 per cent. The predicted reduction in the income of the industry this year may be as high as 20 per cent. The return for the farmer is gradually getting closer and closer to zero. What we need to do here is not, as the previous speaker suggested, to have a Mickey Mouse Bill which helps a few farmers out who are in dire need. We need to look at the basic industry and change it so that it is a continuing industry with a return that is acceptable. We need to establish a base that is stable.
Over the years the Department of Agriculture has shepherded the industry. Since we are getting into such bad shape, we must recognize that that Department has not provided the country with stable marketing and income programs which
Farm Loans Interest Rebate Act
make sense. This very important industry is quickly approaching a debt position where the value of the capital is being very quickly eaten up by the debt.
For years our Party has said that if we had a stable income from farm markets, we would not need the Farm Credit Corporation, or its use could be limited to the development of new farm areas or new industries within the farming context. Our Party feels very strongly that this sector of the economy should be self-sufficient in terms of its refinancing. If we are to continue to have a strong agricultural industry, its profits must be large enough to finance itself through generations. That is not happening.
As I pointed out, a continuous infusion of capital is required to keep this industry going. Over the past eight years, farm debt has been increasing at a very rapid rate. In 1947, payments on interest amounted to $473 million. In 1980 this reached $1.6 billion. That is just the interest to service the debt developed by this industry. The industry should be selfsufficient. However, a large portion of the productivity goes toward servicing the debt.
Maybe this industry is no worse off than the country. The same management which brought this country to the point where it has a $30 billion deficit this year and acumulative deficit of $150 billion has allowed the important agricultural industry to get to the position where it requires a continuous infusion of capital to keep going.
If farm income had increased to the point where the farmer could be assured of a return on production, there would be a little extra for each generation to have the security that is necessary. Instead the Government brings forward a Bill, which I agree is necessary, that only takes care of a very small group of farmers.
Before resuming my seat, I want to point out that although we will support this Bill, we admonish the Government to look at the total agricultural industry and do all that is necessary to put it on the basis where our children and our children's children can depend on a secure farm industry in Canada.
